Internal benchmarking of officers

Source: R/ibench.R
ibench.Rd

Asks whether an officer stops more people of a group (or searches, arrests, uses force more often) than other officers do in the same circumstances. Officers work different places and hours, so each officer's stops are compared not with all other stops but with the other officers' stops weighted to look like this officer's: the propensity e(x) that a stop with circumstances x (place, hour, day, reason) is this officer's comes from a logistic regression on x (over all stops), and each other officer's stop gets the weight `e / (1

  • e), the weights of the effect on the treated (Ridgeway and MacDonald 2009). The benchmark is the weighted share of the outcome among those stops, and the z statistic compares the officer's share with it, with the variance of a proportion for the officer and, for the benchmark, that of a proportion over its effective number of stops, (sum w)^2 / sum w^2. With many officers some will stand out by chance: qis the false discovery rate of Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) over the officers tested, andflagmarks those withqbelowfdr`. (The paper adds a regression adjustment to the weights, a doubly robust estimate, and estimates the local false discovery rate; the plain weights and the step-up rate are used here.)

Usage

ibench(y, off, x = NULL, minn = 20, fdr = 0.05)

Arguments

y

The outcome of each stop: 0 or 1 (or FALSE or TRUE), such as whether the person stopped belongs to the group of interest.

off

The officer of each stop: labels, two officers at least.

x

NULL or the circumstances of each stop: a numeric matrix, a data frame or list of numeric columns, or one numeric vector, one row per stop (code a place or an hour as indicator columns).

minn

The fewest stops of an officer to test: one whole number from 1.

fdr

The false discovery rate at which an officer is flagged: one number strictly between 0 and 1.

Value

An object of class ibench, a list: tab, one row per officer (off, n stops, rate, the officer's share of the outcome, bench, the benchmark, ess, its effective number of stops, z, p, q and flag); fdr; minn; and nx, the number of columns of x.

Details

The comparison is only as good as x: circumstances that differ between officers and are not in x are left in the difference. An officer with fewer than minn stops, or whose propensity model does not converge (circumstances that separate this officer's stops from all others), is not tested (NA).

References

Ridgeway, G. and MacDonald, J. M. (2009). Doubly robust internal benchmarking and false discovery rates for detecting racial bias in police stops. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 104(486), 661-668. doi:10.1198/jasa.2009.0034

Benjamini, Y. and Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate: a practical and powerful approach to multiple testing. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 57(1), 289-300. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x

Examples

set.seed(2)
n <- 3000
off <- sample(sprintf("o%02d", 1:12), n, TRUE)
night <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(off %in% c("o01", "o02"), 0.7, 0.3))
y <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1 + night + 0.8 * (off == "o03")))
ibench(y, off, data.frame(night), minn = 50)
